newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Gaelic games stars paraded alongside professionals.
newsitem.headline: Gaelic games stars paraded alongside professionals.

text.p: Irish sport entered a new age on Wednesday when some of Ireland's leading gaelic games stars were paraded alongside professionals from other sports as clients of a new sports management company.

ProActive Sports Management Ireland Ltd. has concluded deals with individual gaelic games stars which will see the company represent them in all matters relating to sponsorship and other commercial activity.

Among the gaelic games stars who have become clients of the sports management company are gaelic footballers John O'Leary and Jason Sherlock of Dublin, Mark O'Connor of Cork, as well as Kilkenny hurler D.J.Carey.
"We are near completing deals with a number of inter-county teams," Johnny Fortune of ProActive told Reuters.
Jason Sherlock in 1995 became the first player in the history of gaelic games to appoint an agent after he had helped Dublin win the All-Ireland football championship of that year.

The agent he appointed was Kevin Moran, who had worn the Dublin colours himself before he went on to enjoy a highly-successful career as a professional footballer with Manchester United and the Republic of Ireland.
Moran now heads the ProActive marketing team.

The Gaelic Athletic Association, the organisation which governs and administers the rules and regulations of gaelic football and hurling in Ireland, has, since its foundation in 1884 always defended its amateur status staunchly.
But two reports which the GAA themselves commissioned in the last ten years highlighted breaches of its amateur status rules.
The reports showed that teams had been paying coaches while players had been rewarded for making personal appearances at club functions and presentations.

The GAA's reaction after it was revealed in Ireland's Sunday sports newspaper, The Title, that ProActive had approached some of the top gaelic games stars was to release a statement in which it said that a sub-committee would be set up to review the association's existing rules and regulations on amateurism.
The statement went on to say that the Central Council of the GAA wished to advise all players that they should resist any approaches from agents or companies that might endanger their amateur status.
